questions.q: Per this lesson's checklist, what should you confirm about a lineage record's business and technical views?
options: That the business view actually traces back to the technical one, rather than being maintained separately
That only the technical view should ever be created
That the business view should always be longer than the technical view
That the two views must use identical vocabulary
questions.explain: The checklist specifically flags whether the readable business view is actually derived from the detailed technical lineage, rather than drifting apart as separate documentation.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what failure from Lesson 22's case study does the 'column-level, not just table-level' checklist item map to?
options: A table-level arrow alone would have hidden the actual filter-condition bug that undercounted revenue
The POS system crashing during a holiday sale
A customer being charged twice for the same order
A report rendering in the wrong currency
questions.explain: The revenue report case study's root cause was a specific column-level filter condition, invisible at the table-level granularity alone.

questions.q: What checklist item maps directly to the problem uncovered in Lesson 23's customer data case study?
options: Whether there's a clearly designated source of record and matching key when multiple systems hold their own version of the same concept
Whether the lineage diagram uses the color red for warnings
Whether every table in the company has exactly the same number of columns
Whether the report was generated on a Monday or a Friday
questions.explain: Lesson 23's bug came from matching records across systems informally on email address, with no designated authoritative source of record — exactly what this checklist item checks for.

questions.q: What single habit does this lesson identify as common to all three of this chapter's case studies, and as the fix that would have caught each problem earlier?
options: Checking what's downstream before assuming an upstream change is fine
Always rewriting a pipeline from scratch after any bug is found
Never allowing more than one system to store customer data
Switching every report to real-time data instead of batch processing
questions.explain: Each case study involved an upstream change silently breaking an unwritten downstream assumption; checking downstream impact before trusting an upstream change is the habit that catches this earlier.

questions.q: Which course does this lesson identify as next in the Data Governance career path?
options: Master & Reference Data Management
Data Quality Management
Metadata Management & Business Glossary
Data Governance Foundations
questions.explain: The lesson's closing section names Master & Reference Data Management as the next course, framed as solving the source-of-record problem seen in Lesson 23's case study.
